examples.text: The fishermen took pictures of their catch.
The catch amounted to five tons of swordfish.

glosses: A find, in particular a boyfriend or girlfriend or prospective spouse.

examples.text: Did you see his latest catch?
He's a good catch.
"Aaaugh! Just once, I wish I could be considered a catch by men younger than fifty..."

glosses: A stopping mechanism, especially a clasp which stops something from opening.

examples.text: She installed a sturdy catch to keep her cabinets closed tight.

glosses: A hesitation in voice, caused by strong emotion.

examples.text: There was a catch in his voice when he spoke his father's name.

glosses: A concealed difficulty, especially in a deal or negotiation.

examples.text: It sounds like a great idea, but what's the catch?
Be careful, that's a catch question.

glosses: A crick; a sudden muscle pain during unaccustomed positioning when the muscle is in use.

examples.text: I bent over to see under the table and got a catch in my side.

glosses: A fragment of music or poetry.

examples.text: In the lightness of my heart I sang catches of songs as my horse gayly bore me along the well-remembered road.

glosses: A state of readiness to capture or seize; an ambush.

examples.text: You lie at the catch again: this is not for edification.
The common and the canon law […] lie at catch, and wait advantages one against another.

glosses: A crop which has germinated and begun to grow.

examples.text: There was a good catch of rye and a good fall growth.

glosses: A type of strong boat, usually having two masts; a ketch.

examples.text: Fourteene miles Northward from the river Powhatan, is the river Pamaunke, which is navigable 60 or 70 myles, but with Catches and small Barkes 30 or 40 myles farther.

glosses: A type of humorous round in which the voices gradually catch up with one another; usually sung by men and often having bawdy lyrics.

examples.text: Let us be jocund: will you troll the catch / You taught me but while-ere?
One night, I remember, we sang a catch, written (words and music) by Orlo Williams, for three voices.

glosses: The refrain; a line or lines of a song which are repeated from verse to verse.

examples.text: The phrase repeated itself like the catch of a song.

glosses: The act of catching a hit ball before it reaches the ground, resulting in an out.

examples.text: It was he who removed Peter Bowler with the help of a good catch at third slip.

glosses: A player in respect of his catching ability; particularly one who catches well.

examples.text: […] in the field he is all activity, covers an immense amount of ground, and is a sure catch.

glosses: The first contact of an oar with the water.

examples.text: They are sitting up straighter, breaking their arms at the catch and getting on a terrific amount of power at the catch with each stroke.

glosses: A stoppage of breath, resembling a slight cough.

examples.text: When a Scot pronounces water, better, or bottle—wa’er, be’er, or bo’le—the sound is precisely that of the catch; […].

glosses: Passing opportunities seized; snatches.

examples.text: the way it has been writ in, by catches, and many long intervals of interruption

glosses: A slight remembrance; a trace.

examples.text: We retain a catch of those pretty stories.

glosses: To capture, overtake.
To capture or snare (someone or something which would rather escape).

examples.text: I hope I catch a fish.
He ran but we caught him at the exit.
The police caught the robber at a nearby casino.

glosses: To capture, overtake.
To entrap or trip up a person; to deceive.

examples.text: And they send unto him certain of the Pharisees and of the Herodians, to catch him in his words.

glosses: To capture, overtake.

glosses: To capture, overtake.

glosses: To capture, overtake.

examples.text: If you leave now you might catch him.

glosses: To capture, overtake.

glosses: To seize hold of.
To grab, seize, take hold of.

examples.text: I caught her by the arm and turned her to face me.

examples.text: I have to stop for a moment and catch my breath

glosses: To seize hold of.
To grip or entangle.

examples.text: My leg was caught in a tree-root.

glosses: To seize hold of.

examples.text: Be careful your dress doesn't catch on that knob.

glosses: To seize hold of.
To engage with some mechanism; to stick, to succeed in interacting with something or initiating some process.

examples.text: Push it in until it catches.

glosses: To seize hold of.

examples.text: I caught my heel on the threshold.

glosses: To seize hold of.

examples.text: He caught at the railing as he fell.

glosses: To seize hold of.

examples.text: The fire spread slowly until it caught the eaves of the barn.

examples.text: Stop gathering, in that gradual fashion, and catch the water sharply and decisively.

glosses: To seize hold of.

examples.text: The seeds caught and grew.

glosses: To seize hold of.

examples.text: If you are surfing a wave through the rocks, make sure you have a clear route before catching the wave.

glosses: To seize hold of.
To handle an exception.

examples.text: When the program catches an exception, this is recorded in the log file.

glosses: To intercept.
To seize or intercept an object moving through the air (or, sometimes, some other medium).

examples.text: I will throw you the ball, and you catch it.
Watch me catch this raisin in my mouth.

glosses: To intercept.
To seize (an opportunity) when it occurs.

examples.text: she internally resolved henceforward to catch every opportunity of eyeing the hair and of satisfying herself,[…].

glosses: To intercept.
To end a player's innings by catching a hit ball before the first bounce.

examples.text: Townsend hit 29 before he was caught by Wilson.

glosses: To intercept.
To play (a specific period of time) as the catcher.

examples.text: He caught the last three innings.

glosses: To receive (by being in the way).

examples.text: You're going to catch a beating if they find out.

examples.text: The sunlight caught the leaves and the trees turned to gold.
Her hair was caught by the light breeze.

examples.text: Everyone seems to be catching the flu this week.
